summary: Describes how other ARPANET sites could submit batch jobs to the University of California, Santa Barbara computer and fetch the printed results. A program called RJE listened at a published socket, and users needed an account at the UCSB computer center. It is a site-specific service description from 1971, not a general protocol.

plainLanguage.summary: This document explains how to hand a stack of punched-card jobs to a faraway computer at Santa Barbara over the early network, and how to ask it to send the printed results back. It is a set of instructions for one particular machine, not a rule for all computers.

questions: how did ucsb remote job entry work
how to submit batch jobs over the early arpanet
what were the rje input classes
subtitle: How ARPANET sites could submit batch jobs to a UCSB mainframe and fetch the printed output.

tldr.problem: Network users needed exact instructions for sending batch jobs to the University of California, Santa Barbara 360/75 computer and for getting the printed results back.
tldr.mechanism: A process called RJE at socket x'200' accepts files of 80-byte card images in three input classes, and a process called RJOR at socket x'300' returns job output using a flag byte, an 8-byte job name and records marked with op codes.
tldr.outcome: It is a description of one site's service from 1971, not a general protocol, and the unit metadata shows it was updated by RFC 217.

today: The unit metadata gives RFC 105 the status unknown, and lists RFC 217 as an update to it. The text describes a service at one site rather than a general protocol.

sections.title: Remote Job Entry at UCSB
sections.content:
UCSB accepted pseudo card files for batch processing at socket number x'200', site 3. A user first needed an account number from the UCSB Computer Center; during checkout, account #1025 with programmer names such as UCLA, SRI or UTAH could be used. The 360/75 ran under OS MVT and HASP, and an intermediary process called RJE submitted jobs to HASP.

To submit jobs, the user opened a simplex connection to socket x'200' through the Logger. RJE served one user at a time, so the NCP queued any other connection request. Once the connection was made, RJE considered the user logged in. To stop one user from monopolising it, RJE could end a connection if it had to wait more than one minute per record for a transmission. Closing the connection meant end of file, and the user was logged off.
sections.plainLanguage: One job slot was shared by everyone. If someone else was using it, you waited in line, and the service could drop you if you went quiet for too long.

sections.title: The Three Input Classes
sections.content:
RJE expected the first byte it received to be zeros, meaning message Type 0, and after that it ignored IMP-message boundaries. The second byte declared the input class, and that choice held for the whole connection: 00 for Class A (stream-oriented), 10 for Class B (variable-length record) and 11 for Class C (fixed-length record).

Whatever the class, the file was sent as card images, each padded or truncated to 80 bytes, structured exactly as if placed on the card reader. A job card and the usual job control language cards had to be present. A job needing special disks or tapes required a /*SETUP card right after its job card. In Class A the third byte was a break character that ended each card image. In Class B each record began with op code x'01' and a two-byte length in bits, a multiple of 8. In Class C the file was simply a run of 80-byte card images.
sections.plainLanguage: You could tell the computer three ways how your cards were packed: separated by a special mark, each with a length printed in front, or all exactly the same size.

sections.title: Fetching Output with RJOR
sections.content:
Class A SYSOUT output from jobs submitted through RJE could be fetched from socket x'300', site 3, provided the character T had appeared as the eighth positional accounting parameter on the job card. A process called RJOR answered there and carried out the request.

The user opened a full duplex connection and sent, over the Input Connection, a flag byte followed by an 8-byte EBCDIC job name. The flag bits were: bit 0 transmit the output, bit 1 purge the output, bit 2 wait as long as needed, and bit 3 cancel an earlier wait request. RJOR then replied over a second connection, from its socket x'301' to the user's socket one less than the one used to reach it, sending the job name and then logical records. Each record had a one-byte op code, a two-byte length and the text. Op code x'01' carried one output record; the other defined op codes, 00 through 0B, reported events such as end of file, purged output, I/O errors and waiting for output.
sections.plainLanguage: To get your results you sent a small slip naming the job and what you wanted done. The computer then sent the printout, or a note saying why it could not yet.

items.label: End-of-File
items.desc: All output from the job has been transmitted.

items.label: Output
items.desc: The text field holds one record of a SYSOUT data set.

items.label: Output file purged
items.desc: Output from the job has been purged as requested.

items.label: Waiting for output
items.desc: Output is not available and the wait-for-output option was specified.

items.label: Request canceled
items.desc: A previous wait request was canceled at the user's request.

items.desc: No output was found and the wait option was not specified.
